description:
We're interested in technology, AI, multimedia, and creative problem-solving. Our team brings skills in video editing, visual storytelling, data analysis, and UI/UX design.

We're looking for motivated team members with skills in programming, AI, scientific research, physics, and astrophysics to complement our strengths and help us build an innovative solution together!
summary:
NASA’s microgravity combustion research provides evidence on flammability, flame behaviour, smoke detection, and fire suppression. Yet records, datasets, and publications are spread across resources, making evidence difficult to find and compare for spacecraft and habitat safety.

FLAME Intelligence is an AI-powered dashboard connected to NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI). It brings combustion investigations into one workspace to search studies, inspect experimental conditions and measurements, compare results, and explore relevance to spacecraft, stations, lunar or Martian habitats, and pressurized rovers.

The AI Research Assistant answers natural-language questions with concise explanations linked to original sources. Transparent evidence-based ranking explains why studies match a scenario, where conditions differ, and which data are missing. Evidence-gap analysis highlights underrepresented conditions.

The platform will organize PSI metadata through shared data models and APIs. A responsive Next.js, React, and TypeScript interface will integrate search, comparison, visualizations, and AI services. Testing will check usability, accuracy, traceability, and failure handling.

FLAME Intelligence simplifies research discovery while separating measured results, metadata, and AI interpretation. It helps researchers, engineers, educators, and students assess evidence without presenting AI conclusions as experimental facts or rankings as certified fire-risk predictions.
details:
OrbitFlame

What does the project do and how does it work?

OrbitFlame is a research and decision-support platform focused on fire safety in spacecraft and space habitats. It uses real experimental data from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository to make combustion and flammability research from spaceflight and ground-based experiments easier to explore, compare, and understand.

The platform organizes data from 20 NASA investigations, including BASS, Saffire, ACME, FLEX, and SAME. It brings this information together through several interactive features.

The Research Library allows users to browse original NASA investigation records, experimental tables, test matrices, and hardware descriptions. The Data Explorer provides access to individual test runs and their recorded conditions, including fuel type, pressure, oxygen concentration, airflow, and experimental outcomes.

A built-in Unit Conversion Tool converts compatible physical quantities into SI units while retaining their original reported values. It ensures that only quantities of the same type are compared, such as pressure with pressure.

The Habitat Ranking feature compares NASA experiments with different environments, including the International Space Station, lunar and Mars habitats, spacesuits, and Earth-based analogs. Each investigation receives a relevance score from 0 to 100 based on atmospheric conditions, airflow, gravity, and fuel type.

OrbitFlame also includes flammability and extinction prediction models trained on real NASA experimental data. Predictions are displayed only when the models perform better than a simple baseline in validation tests where entire experiments are held out.

The AI Assistant answers questions using only the indexed NASA investigations. It links its responses to their original source records, preserves reported units, and avoids making claims that cannot be supported by the available evidence.

Missing information is never silently estimated. When a NASA record does not report a value, OrbitFlame identifies it as blank or "not reported."

What benefits does it have?

OrbitFlame makes a large and technically complex collection of NASA fire-safety research easier to access and use. Researchers, students, engineers, and educators can explore relevant information without manually searching through multiple files and investigation records.

By combining experimental data with analytical tools, the platform helps users compare research findings and identify experiments that may be relevant to specific space environments. Its results are transparent: users can trace information back to the original NASA records and review measured values, model outputs, and comparable experiments.

The platform also makes uncertainty easier to understand. It distinguishes between recorded measurements, model predictions, inferred gravity conditions, and missing information. Its AI assistant provides source-based answers rather than unsupported conclusions.

Together, these features support more informed research and planning while making clear that predictions are not safety certifications.

What is the intended impact of the project?

OrbitFlame aims to improve how space-fire-safety research is discovered, compared, and interpreted. As human missions move toward longer stays on the Moon and Mars, understanding how fire behaves under different atmospheric and gravity conditions becomes increasingly important.

The platform helps users identify which existing NASA experiments are most relevant to a particular habitat, where experimental evidence is available, and where further research may be needed. It can also highlight materials, atmospheric conditions, and airflow ranges that deserve additional testing.

By making research gaps and data limitations easier to identify, OrbitFlame supports better research planning and helps direct attention toward areas where more experimental evidence is needed.

Ultimately, the project aims to contribute to safer spacecraft and space habitats by making reliable scientific evidence more accessible and easier to interpret.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software were used?

The project uses experimental tables and investigation records from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics repository. Its main technical components include data organization and indexing, unit-conversion logic, statistical models for flammability and extinction estimates, a habitat-matching and scoring system, and an AI assistant that retrieves information from indexed research records.

AI-powered tools also played an important role in the development process. Claude, Gemini, and ChatGPT were used to support coding, problem-solving, research, and technical writing. Manus AI was used to assist with video creation and visual presentation of the project.

The project combines NASA experimental data with AI-assisted development and analytical approaches to create an interactive research platform.

The available project documentation does not specify the exact programming languages, frameworks, databases, statistical libraries, hosting environment, or hardware used during development.

How is the project creative?

OrbitFlame turns scattered scientific records into an interactive platform that supports research and practical decision-making. Rather than simply displaying NASA data, it brings together scientific data exploration, habitat similarity scoring, unit-aware comparisons, statistical predictions, and AI-powered research assistance.

One of its distinctive features is the way it approaches gravity comparisons. NASA PSI tables do not always provide a direct gravity measurement, so OrbitFlame uses investigation flight records and airflow-equivalent behavior to support cautious comparisons. For lunar and Martian environments, the results are clearly presented as indicative because the indexed PSI experiments were not conducted at exactly the Moon's or Mars's gravity.

The project also places strong emphasis on scientific reliability. It does not fill in missing values, treat similar experiments as proof of safety, or present model predictions as guarantees. This approach combines innovation with responsible use of scientific data and AI.

What factors did the team consider?

The team considered scientific accuracy, data reliability, model performance, and the potential safety implications of the platform.

All experimental values are retained as reported by NASA, including their original units. Unit conversions are performed only between compatible physical quantities, and missing values remain unreported rather than being estimated.

Model reliability was another important consideration. Predictions are shown only when the models outperform a basic baseline during validation using held-out experiments. The platform also distinguishes between measured results, inferred information, and model estimates so users can understand the limitations of each result.

Source traceability is maintained throughout the system. AI responses and analytical results are connected to the relevant NASA records, allowing users to review the evidence behind them.

The team also considered the practical conditions that influence fire behavior in spacecraft and habitats, including oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow, fuel type, and gravity. Particular care was taken to avoid making unsupported safety claims, such as declaring a material safe or assuming a fire suppressant will work based on a similar experiment.

Finally, the platform distinguishes between a lack of indexed data and proof that no research exists. This helps users recognize research gaps without drawing conclusions that the available evidence cannot support.

OrbitFlame is designed to make space-fire-safety research more accessible while demonstrating how scientific data and AI can be combined in a transparent, careful, and responsible way.
